title: I Observe More Than I Speak.
subtitle: Two hours a day, a window seat, and the lives of strangers who remind me how much I already have.
excerpt: My college is an hour away from home, which means I spend two hours of my day travelling to a place where I probably learn nothing. I still go, of course. Attendance, haha. But somewhere between the familiar roads, forgotten earphones, and strangers carrying invisible burdens, I have started learning something I was never going to find in a classroom.

content.lead: I observe more than I speak. I think I have always been that way, but I started noticing it properly during my daily commute to college.

sections.heading: Two hours of my life. Every single day.
paragraphs: My college is roughly an hour away from where I live. So that is two hours of my life every day, spent travelling to college and back, where I will probably learn nothing particularly memorable. Yet I continue doing it. For attendance, of course. Haha.

There is something hilariously tragic about waking up early, getting ready, travelling for an hour, sitting through lectures, travelling another hour back home, and then opening YouTube to learn the things I was supposedly supposed to learn in college.
But somewhere along the way, the commute itself became interesting.

Instead of spending the entire journey scrolling through Instagram Reels, watching strangers dance for fifteen seconds, or consuming content I will forget before the next station, I started putting my phone away. Not every day, obviously. I am still human, and the algorithm knows exactly how to get me.
Sometimes I just sit there. Sometimes I listen to music. And sometimes, when I have forgotten my earphones at home, I have no choice but to listen to the world around me.
Honestly, those forgotten-earphone days have given me some of my favourite little moments.

sections.heading: The window seat.
paragraphs: I have always preferred the window seat. There is something about looking outside while the world moves past you that makes it easier to sit with your own thoughts. Buildings blur into one another, familiar streets appear and disappear, people hurry towards places you will probably never visit, and life continues in a thousand different directions at once.
I can spend an entire journey looking outside without feeling the need to do anything. No music. No phone. No particular thought that I am trying to finish. Just watching.
And when I do turn my attention towards the people around me, I realise how much is happening in the same small space.

There is someone staring at their phone, repeatedly opening the same chat. Someone sitting quietly with their head against the window. Someone looking exhausted in a way that sleep alone probably cannot fix. Someone smiling at a message that has clearly made their entire day.
I do not know their stories. I cannot pretend to. But sometimes, the little things people do make you wonder what might be happening in their lives beyond the few minutes you get to see them.

Maybe someone beside me has just gone through a breakup. Maybe somebody has lost their job. Maybe someone has failed an examination they spent months preparing for. Maybe someone is returning home after the worst day they have had in years.
Or maybe they are simply tired and want to get home. That is possible too.
We pass hundreds of people without ever knowing what they are carrying. We see faces, clothes, expressions, and brief moments of behaviour. We rarely see the entire story behind them.

Sometimes I look at someone and wonder what their life looks like when they are not sitting in front of me. Who are they going home to? What are they worried about? What are they looking forward to? What is the one thing they wish would finally work out?

It is strange to think that every person around you has an entire life of their own. Their own childhood, their own favourite songs, their own embarrassing memories, their own heartbreaks, their own private jokes, their own people, and their own reasons for getting out of bed in the morning.
And for a brief moment, all those separate lives happen to occupy the same train compartment.

sections.heading: The things you notice when you stop looking at a screen.
paragraphs: Every now and then, somebody walks through the compartment selling something. Sometimes it is a small item nobody particularly needs. Sometimes it is food. Sometimes it is a person asking for money.

I remember noticing a man with only one leg trying to sell things to people passing by. I have also seen children approaching passengers, asking for money, sometimes crying as they try to explain their situation.
Those moments stay with me longer than I expect them to.

I am not going to pretend that I know their entire circumstances just because I saw them for a few minutes. I do not know their histories, the choices that brought them there, or the things they have endured. I cannot reduce a stranger’s entire life to the most difficult moment I happen to witness.
But I can recognise that there are people around me dealing with circumstances I have never had to think about in the same way.

I can sit in a compartment, complain about the heat, worry about attendance, get irritated because my train is late, and spend the journey thinking about a deadline. Someone else might be spending that same journey trying to earn enough money to get through the day.
The contrast is difficult to ignore.

And it makes me think about how easily I complain about my own life. A bad grade, a stressful week, a project that refuses to work, an argument with someone I care about, or a day that does not go according to plan can make everything feel unnecessarily heavy.

Those feelings are real. I do not think we should invalidate our own struggles just because somebody else has it worse. Pain is not a competition, and gratitude should not require us to pretend that our problems do not exist.
But perspective matters. Sometimes, you need a reminder that the things frustrating you today are happening alongside things other people are struggling to survive.
It does not make your problems disappear. It changes the way you hold them.

sections.heading: I think I have a lot to be grateful for.
paragraphs: I often find myself feeling grateful during these journeys. Grateful to God for the life I have been given, for the opportunities available to me, for the people who care about me, and for the simple fact that I can spend two hours complaining about travelling to college instead of worrying about where my next meal will come from.

I have a home to return to. I have the opportunity to study. I have a phone that I can complain about being addicted to, earphones that I occasionally forget, and the freedom to spend a journey looking out of a window without having to turn every minute into something productive.
These things sound ordinary because they have become ordinary to me.

And perhaps that is the problem. We become so accustomed to the things that make our lives comfortable that we stop noticing them. We notice the things we lack far more quickly than the things we already have.

We compare ourselves with someone who has a better phone, a better college, a better job, more money, more achievements, or a life that looks considerably more exciting on Instagram. There is always somebody who appears to be doing better. Always another milestone to chase, another reason to feel behind, another version of ourselves that we think we should have become by now.
Meanwhile, there are things about our present lives that another person might quietly wish for.

The education we complain about. The family members whose calls we sometimes ignore. The ordinary evening at home that feels unremarkable until it becomes a memory. The ability to travel somewhere without calculating every rupee. The chance to make mistakes while still having people and opportunities to fall back on.

I am not saying this to make anybody feel guilty for wanting more. Ambition is not a bad thing. I have things I want to achieve, places I want to go, and a life I want to build. I am not going to stop wanting those things.
I just do not want to become so obsessed with the life I am trying to build that I forget to appreciate the life I am already living.
Because, honestly, what more can I ask for at this very moment? Not because my life is perfect, but because it has already given me so much that I sometimes forget to acknowledge.

sections.heading: Someone else might be dreaming of the life I complain about.
paragraphs: This thought follows me home sometimes.

I complain about the two-hour commute. Somebody else might be wishing they had the opportunity to attend college at all. I get annoyed about examinations. Somebody else might be wishing they had the chance to sit in a classroom and worry about their marks. I think about my future and feel anxious about whether I will become the person I want to be. Somebody else might be fighting for a chance to have the choices I currently take for granted.
I could be living a version of someone else’s dream life without even realising it.
That sentence sounds dramatic, but sit with it for a moment.

There are people who would love to have the opportunities you casually dismiss, the stability you barely notice, or the freedom you assume will always be there. There are things you have today that a younger version of yourself once wanted desperately. Things you worked for, things somebody helped you achieve, and things you received without ever having to ask.

And yet, the human mind is remarkably talented at moving the finish line. We achieve something, feel happy about it for a little while, and then immediately start looking at what comes next. The new thing becomes normal. The old thing becomes irrelevant. Gratitude is replaced by the next goal before we have properly appreciated the last one.
I do it too. I would be lying if I said otherwise.

I want to do well in my career. I want to build things that matter. I want to travel, experience more of the world, meet interesting people, and become someone I can be proud of. There is nothing wrong with wanting a bigger life.
But I am slowly learning that a bigger life and an appreciated life are not necessarily the same thing.
You can keep moving forward without treating your present as something you need to escape. You can want more without convincing yourself that what you have is not enough to be thankful for.

sections.heading: There is an entire world happening around us.
paragraphs: Perhaps that is what I like most about observing people. It reminds me that my perspective is only one small part of a much larger world.

When something goes wrong in my life, it can feel like the entire world has decided to inconvenience me personally. A bad day becomes the worst day. A setback starts looking like a permanent failure. One disappointing moment can occupy so much space in my head that I forget everything else that is still going right.
Then I look up.

Someone is laughing at a joke on their phone. A parent is trying to keep a sleepy child awake. Two friends are talking animatedly about something I will never know. An elderly person is carefully making their way towards the door. Someone is staring outside, perhaps thinking about the exact same things I am thinking about.
Life is happening to all of them, too.

Their joys do not disappear because I am having a difficult day. Their difficulties do not disappear because I am having a good one. Everyone is moving through something, and most of it will remain invisible to the strangers sitting beside them.

I find that thought strangely comforting. Not because suffering is good, but because it reminds me that I am not the centre of every story. My problems matter, but they are not the only problems that exist. My ambitions matter, but there are millions of other people trying to make something of their lives, too.

It makes me a little more patient with people. A little less certain that I understand what somebody else is going through. A little more willing to leave room for the possibility that there is a story behind a behaviour I do not understand.

The person who seems rude might be having a terrible day. The person who looks distracted might be worrying about someone they love. The person who appears to have everything figured out might be struggling with something they have told nobody.
Of course, not every expression hides a tragedy. Not every stranger needs to be turned into a philosophical lesson. Sometimes a person is just looking out of a window because the view is nice.
I think the point is simply that we do not know enough to be so quick to judge.

sections.heading: Maybe the journey is teaching me something after all.
paragraphs: It is funny. I began this by saying that I spend two hours every day travelling to college, where I probably learn nothing.
Maybe I should take that back.

I am not saying that watching people on a train can replace an education. It cannot. I still need to attend my lectures, learn my subjects, complete my projects, and figure out what I want to do with my life. And yes, attendance still matters. Haha.
But there are things you begin to notice when you allow yourself to be present instead of constantly trying to fill every quiet moment with something else.

You notice the world outside the window. You notice the people sitting beside you. You notice how much you have, how little you know about the lives of others, and how quickly your own worries can make you forget both.

You realise that not every moment needs to be productive. You do not have to turn every train ride into a podcast session, every walk into a phone call, or every quiet minute into an opportunity to improve yourself. Sometimes, doing absolutely nothing gives you the space to notice something you would otherwise miss.

I still scroll through reels. I still complain about the commute. I still get frustrated about things that, in retrospect, are not particularly important. I am not writing this as someone who has mastered gratitude or figured out the secret to being content.
I am just someone who occasionally puts his phone away, looks out of a window, and comes home thinking a little differently than he did that morning.

sections.heading: Before I get back to scrolling.
paragraphs: I do not know the people I see during my daily commute. Most of them will remain strangers. I will probably never find out what happened to the person staring at their phone, whether the exhausted passenger finally got some rest, or whether the person who seemed to be having a terrible day eventually had a better evening.
I will never know the full stories behind those faces, and perhaps I am not supposed to.

But I can carry something away from those brief encounters. A little perspective. A little humility. A reminder that the world is bigger than my immediate concerns and that the ordinary things in my life are not necessarily ordinary to everyone.

I can be grateful without pretending that suffering does not exist. I can want more from life without despising the life I already have. I can recognise my privileges without feeling guilty for things I did not choose, and perhaps use the opportunities I have been given to do something worthwhile with them.
And I can try to be a little kinder, because I will never know what somebody else is carrying when they sit down beside me.
Tomorrow, I will probably wake up, get ready, travel for an hour, complain about attendance, and do it all over again.
Maybe I will remember my earphones. Maybe I will not.
Either way, I hope I remember to look outside once in a while.
Because somewhere between the station I leave from and the one I arrive at, there is an entire world passing me by. And I do not want to spend my whole life looking down at a screen while it does.

I have a long way to go. There is so much I want to experience, learn, build, and become. But for a little while, on an ordinary journey to an ordinary college, I can look out of a window and appreciate the fact that I am here at all.
And maybe, for today, that is enough.

title: The Audacity to Blame Everything on Women.
subtitle: We worship goddesses, question survivors, and still wonder why women do not feel safe.
excerpt: Every year, we worship goddesses, celebrate women as symbols of strength, and speak about respecting them. Yet when a woman is raped, assaulted, or killed, one of the first things people want to know is what she was wearing. At what point did we decide that a woman must justify her existence before she deserves to be safe?

content.lead: It is Navratri. Somewhere in India, people are decorating temples, fasting, dancing to garba, bringing home idols of goddesses, and praying to the divine feminine. We fold our hands before Durga, the goddess who destroys evil. We celebrate strength, courage, motherhood, and the power of women. And then, somewhere else in the same country, a woman is being told that her clothes were too revealing. That she should not have been out so late. That she should have known better. That she somehow invited what happened to her. I genuinely want to understand how we manage to hold these two ideas in our heads at the same time. How do we worship the divine feminine while treating actual women as though their safety is a privilege they have to earn?

sections.heading: 1. We worship her in a temple. We question her on the street.
paragraphs: There is something deeply uncomfortable about the timing of this conversation. During Navratri, we celebrate a goddess powerful enough to defeat demons. We teach children stories about her strength. We put her image on posters, sing songs in her honour, and participate in traditions that have been passed down for generations.

And yet, when it comes to women who exist outside our religious imagination, the respect suddenly becomes conditional. Respect her, provided she dresses appropriately. Respect her, provided she does not speak too loudly. Respect her, provided she does not come home late, drink, date, reject someone, or make decisions that somebody else considers unacceptable.
What exactly are we worshipping if the respect disappears the moment a woman stops behaving according to our expectations?

I am not questioning anyone’s faith or suggesting that religious traditions are responsible for sexual violence. I am questioning the hypocrisy of celebrating the idea of womanhood while refusing to respect the autonomy of women themselves.

A goddess does not have to explain why she is wearing what she is wearing. She does not have to prove that she is respectable before she deserves protection. She does not have to submit a character certificate to be treated with dignity.
Neither should an actual woman.

sections.heading: 2. The question that should make us ashamed
paragraphs: A woman is raped, and the questions begin.

What was she wearing? Why was she out at that hour? Why did she go there? Why was she alone? Why was she talking to him? Why was she drinking? Why did she trust him? Why did she not fight back? Why did she not report it immediately?

Notice how quickly the conversation moves away from the person who committed the violence and towards the person who suffered it. Suddenly, everyone becomes an investigator of her decisions, her character, her relationships, her photographs, her clothing, and her entire life before the incident.
We examine her behaviour with a microscope while the behaviour of the accused becomes a debate about circumstances, temptation, anger, alcohol, upbringing, or what she supposedly did to provoke him.

Let us make something painfully clear. Wearing short clothes is not consent. Being outside at midnight is not consent. Drinking alcohol is not consent. Being in a relationship is not consent. Having consensual sex with someone in the past does not mean consenting to it today. Flirting is not consent. Rejecting someone does not make you responsible for their reaction.

Consent is not a reward a person earns by behaving according to society’s rules. It is not a prize that can be claimed because somebody feels entitled to it. And it certainly does not become optional because another person is attracted to you.

A person can make an unwise decision and still have the right not to be assaulted. A person can trust the wrong individual and still have the right not to be betrayed. A person can make mistakes without surrendering their basic human rights.
Why is this so difficult for us to understand?

sections.heading: 3. The numbers are not just numbers
paragraphs: Sometimes, people need statistics before they are willing to accept the scale of a problem. So let us look at what the reporting tells us.

A [Reuters report](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/brutal-killing-11-year-old-highlights-unrelenting-sexual-violence-india-2026-07-15/) published on 15 July 2026, citing government data, stated that India recorded 29,536 rape cases in 2024. That is more than 80 registered cases a day. The report also noted 69,191 cases registered under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act in 2024. These are registered cases, not a complete count of every incident of sexual violence that occurred.

Read those numbers again. Behind every registered case is a human being whose life may have been changed by someone else’s decision to violate them. There may be a family trying to understand what happened, a survivor trying to rebuild a sense of safety, or a child who should have been worrying about school, friendships, and ordinary childhood things instead.

In June 2026, the [Centre for Economic Data and Analysis (CEDA) at Ashoka University](https://ceda.ashoka.edu.in/what-indias-2024-crime-statistics-reveal-and-miss-about-violence-against-women/) examined the latest [NCRB](https://ncrb.gov.in/) statistics available at the time. Its analysis reported 4,41,534 registered crimes against women in India in 2024, averaging approximately 1,210 cases a day. It also explained why official figures cannot capture the full extent of violence: an incident must be reported, registered, and classified within the criminal justice system to appear in those statistics.

The report also highlights a difficult reality: violence against women is not confined to strangers in dark streets. In 96.8 percent of rape cases registered in 2024, the accused was known to the survivor, according to the analysis. That challenges the comforting idea that danger always comes from some unfamiliar person lurking outside.

ThePrint’s September 2026 [reporting on sexual violence at educational institutions](https://theprint.in/feature/indian-colleges-women-students-history-campus-rapes/3056085/) described cases and allegations spanning multiple campuses, including incidents that raised questions about institutional responses and survivor treatment. A college is supposed to be a place where young people learn, grow, and prepare for their futures. What does it mean when the very institutions entrusted with their education struggle to ensure their safety?

In October 2026, [Moneycontrol reported](https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/india/2454-rape-cases-in-five-months-tmc-attacks-bjp-over-west-bengal-law-and-order-14046870.html) that the Trinamool Congress cited figures it attributed to West Bengal’s State Crime Records Bureau, claiming that 2,454 rape cases had been registered in the state over five months. That figure appeared in a political dispute over law and order. It should be understood as a claim attributed to the party in that report, not as an independently verified national statistic.

The politics around these numbers will continue. Governments will blame previous governments. Opposition parties will point fingers. Leaders will make promises, announce measures, and demand accountability from their rivals.

Fine. Political accountability matters. But a woman’s safety should not become a talking point that matters only when the right party is in opposition. Sexual violence is not a partisan inconvenience. It is a human rights issue, and no political slogan is a substitute for a system that actually protects people.

sections.heading: 4. Can we please stop asking women to solve a problem they did not create?
paragraphs: This is the part that genuinely angers me.

A girl is told to dress modestly because men might get distracted. She is told not to go out alone because men might take advantage. She is told to share her live location, carry her keys between her fingers, avoid certain streets, avoid certain people, avoid certain hours, and always remain alert.

Women are taught to plan their lives around the possibility that someone might hurt them. They memorise precautions that many men never have to consider before leaving the house. They learn to send messages when they reach home, pretend to be on phone calls while walking alone, and think twice about accepting an ordinary ride or taking an ordinary route.

And yes, personal safety precautions can sometimes be useful. Nobody should be criticised for taking measures that help them feel safer. But why have we become so comfortable treating these precautions as the primary solution?
Why is the girl responsible for making sure she is never in a vulnerable situation, while the boy is not equally expected to understand that another person’s vulnerability is not an opportunity?
Why do we keep telling women how to avoid being assaulted instead of putting the same energy into teaching people not to assault others?

And before somebody responds with the usual argument that men face dangers too, yes, men can be victims of sexual violence as well. Their experiences deserve to be taken seriously, and they should never be mocked or dismissed. Acknowledging that does not erase the specific ways women experience gendered violence or make victim-blaming acceptable.
Safety advice can reduce some risks. It cannot transfer responsibility for a crime from the person who commits it to the person who suffers it.
A woman should not have to live a perfectly calculated life to deserve an ordinary one.

sections.heading: 5. Can you teach your son some basic human decency?
paragraphs: Let me ask a question that should not be controversial.

When parents teach their children how to speak, how to behave in public, how to respect their elders, how to share, and how to distinguish right from wrong, why does respecting another person’s boundaries somehow become optional?

Can you teach your son that a woman does not owe him attention because he bought her a gift? That rejection is not humiliation? That being attracted to someone does not give him a claim over them? That persistence is not romantic when the other person has already said no? That a relationship does not give him permanent access to another person’s body?
Can you tell him to keep his hands to himself? To understand the word no? To stop treating women as prizes to be won, possessions to be controlled, or obstacles to be overcome when they refuse him?

And if he does something wrong, can you hold him accountable instead of immediately looking for an excuse? Can you resist the instinct to blame the girl, question her character, or insist that your son could never have done such a thing simply because he is your son?

I am not suggesting that sexual violence can be explained by bad parenting alone. People are shaped by social attitudes, peer groups, institutions, power, and individual choices. Nor is every parent responsible for the criminal actions of an adult child. But families are one of the places where children first learn what respect looks like, and they have a role in challenging entitlement rather than excusing it.

We teach children not to steal because another person’s belongings are not theirs. We teach them not to hit someone because anger does not justify violence. We should teach them that another person’s body, choices, and boundaries deserve the same fundamental respect.

And this responsibility does not belong to parents alone. Schools, colleges, workplaces, communities, religious institutions, and the justice system all have a role in creating a culture where consent is understood, misconduct is taken seriously, and survivors are not punished for speaking up.
The conversation cannot end with telling girls how to protect themselves. It has to include teaching boys and men that other people are not responsible for managing their behaviour.

sections.heading: 6. What happens after she speaks up?
paragraphs: Imagine finding the courage to tell people that something terrible has happened to you. You might already be frightened, confused, traumatised, or unsure about what happens next. You might be worried about your family, your education, your job, your relationships, or whether anybody will believe you.
And then you discover that speaking up can bring its own punishment.

People question why you did not report it earlier. They ask why you were with the person in the first place. They scrutinise your messages and photographs. They spread rumours, demand details, and discuss your experience as if your worst moment has become public property.

Sometimes, the institution that should protect you worries more about its reputation. Sometimes, people around you pressure you to remain silent because the truth would be inconvenient. Sometimes, the public becomes so obsessed with the identity of the accused, their social standing, or their political connections that the person who suffered the violence disappears from the conversation.

ThePrint’s [reporting on campus cases](https://theprint.in/feature/indian-colleges-women-students-history-campus-rapes/3056085/) also highlighted how a survivor’s character and alleged sexual history have entered legal discussions. That is precisely why the treatment of survivors matters alongside the investigation itself. A person’s sexual history or perceived respectability should not become a shortcut for dismissing an allegation.

Every case must be investigated fairly. An allegation should not replace evidence, and every accused person is entitled to due process. Justice requires careful investigation, competent policing, and courts that examine the evidence. Taking sexual violence seriously does not mean abandoning fairness.

But fairness is not the same as humiliating survivors. Due process is not an invitation to conduct a public character assassination. And the presumption of innocence is not a licence for society to treat every person who reports sexual violence as a liar.

We need investigations that are prompt and competent, institutions that take complaints seriously, protection from retaliation, support for survivors, and a justice system capable of delivering outcomes without making people wait indefinitely.
If we want people to report sexual violence, we cannot build a culture in which reporting it becomes another thing they have to survive.

sections.heading: 7. Safety is not a favour
paragraphs: There is a tendency to talk about women’s safety as though it were a special concession society is expected to provide. We discuss whether women should be allowed to travel late, whether they should live alone, whether they should drink, whether they should wear certain clothes, whether they should be allowed to make particular choices.
But safety is not a reward for obedience. It is not a privilege reserved for women who satisfy somebody’s definition of a good daughter, a good girlfriend, a good wife, or a good woman.
It is a basic expectation of living in a society that claims to value human dignity.

No woman should have to prove that she is respectable before the police take her complaint seriously. No child should have to understand the dangers of the world before the adults around them take responsibility for protecting them. No student should have to wonder whether reporting misconduct will cost them their education or reputation.
And no family should have to choose between seeking justice and protecting themselves from the social consequences of speaking out.

That requires more than outrage after a horrific case becomes national news. It requires effective policing, functioning institutions, timely investigations, fair trials, accountability for negligence, better consent education, and social attitudes that stop treating women’s autonomy as a threat.

It also requires us to stop confusing punishment after a crime with prevention before one. Justice matters enormously, but so does building a society in which people learn to respect boundaries long before a courtroom becomes involved.

We cannot promise that every crime will be prevented. No country can. But we can decide that the response to sexual violence will not be to shame the person who experienced it, protect powerful people from scrutiny, or quietly move on once the headlines disappear.

sections.heading: 8. During Navratri, perhaps we should ask ourselves what we are celebrating.
paragraphs: I keep returning to that contradiction. We celebrate the goddess who defeats evil, but do we have the courage to confront the attitudes that allow evil to hide behind ordinary conversations?

We sing about strength while telling women to make themselves smaller. We celebrate feminine power while policing feminine freedom. We speak about honour while placing the burden of family honour on women’s bodies. We tell our daughters to be careful, our sisters to stay alert, our girlfriends to share their locations, and our wives to adjust.

But how often do we tell our sons, brothers, friends, and ourselves to examine the entitlement we have learned? How often do we challenge the friend who makes a degrading joke, the relative who blames a survivor, or the person who insists that a woman must have done something to deserve what happened to her?

Culture is not changed by a festival alone. It changes through the ordinary things people choose to tolerate, challenge, teach, and refuse to excuse. It changes when respect is practised even when nobody is watching and when accountability applies even to people we love.

I do not believe that every man is a threat, and I do not believe that every woman experiences the world in the same way. I do believe that a society serious about safety has to be willing to confront uncomfortable patterns rather than dismiss them because they challenge our self-image.

If our reverence for women exists only when they are represented as goddesses, mothers, daughters, or symbols of purity, then perhaps what we are respecting is not women themselves, but the roles we have assigned to them.

Real respect begins when a woman is allowed to be an ordinary human being. Imperfect. Independent. Loud. Quiet. Out late. In love. Out of love. Wearing whatever she wants. Making decisions we agree with and decisions we do not. Saying yes when she wants to and no when she does not.
None of those things should determine whether she deserves to be safe.

sections.heading: I am tired of asking women what they could have done differently.
paragraphs: I want us to ask different questions.

Why was the complaint not investigated properly? Why did the institution fail to protect its students? Why did the system take so long to respond? Why was the survivor subjected to humiliation? Why was the accused able to exploit a position of power? What could have prevented this? What needs to change so that the next person is safer?
And when we hear someone blame a woman for the violence committed against her, I want us to challenge that instinct instead of letting it pass as common sense.
Because there is something profoundly wrong with a society that expects women to spend their lives calculating how not to be harmed, then judges them when those calculations fail.

You should not need to dress a certain way, live a certain way, speak a certain way, or make every possible precaution to deserve the most basic form of security. You should not have to be someone’s daughter, someone’s sister, someone’s mother, or someone’s goddess to have your humanity recognised.
You should be safe because you are a human being. That should be enough.
This Navratri, we will once again bow before the goddess. We will celebrate her courage, her strength, and her victory over evil.
I hope we can find the courage to carry some of that respect beyond the temple doors.
Because a country that knows how to worship women should also learn how to protect them.

sections.heading: Sources & Further Reading
paragraphs: The reporting and data below provide context for the incidents, registered crime figures, campus safety concerns, and institutional issues discussed in this article. The personal reflections and moral arguments are my own.

1. [Reuters — Brutal killing of 11-year-old highlights unrelenting sexual violence in India](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/brutal-killing-11-year-old-highlights-unrelenting-sexual-violence-india-2026-07-15/) (15 July 2026). Reporting on a child’s rape and murder, registered rape cases in India, offences against children, and continuing concerns about sexual violence. [https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/brutal-killing-11-year-old-highlights-unrelenting-sexual-violence-india-2026-07-15/](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/brutal-killing-11-year-old-highlights-unrelenting-sexual-violence-india-2026-07-15/)

2. [ThePrint — Indian colleges keep failing women students.
