title: Why Elon Musk Has Balls of Steel
subtitle: From ranting online to making science fiction look like an engineering problem.
excerpt: The internet has spent years laughing at Elon Musk. Then he showed us a car performing airborne manoeuvres with rocket-inspired technology. I think we underestimate what it takes to attempt something most people would not even dare to imagine.

content.lead: The internet has spent years making fun of Elon Musk. And, to be fair, the man has given it plenty of material. The tweets, the deadlines, the promises, the occasional announcement that makes you wonder whether someone accidentally gave the world’s richest man access to his own shower thoughts. But then you look up and discover that he is trying to put rocket technology into a fucking car. Suddenly, the joke gets a little more complicated.

sections.heading: 1. The man is trying to make a car fly. Seriously.
paragraphs: On October 15, 2026, Tesla finally showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster, and the demonstration was absolutely ridiculous in the best possible way. The car drove up a curved ramp, performed an airborne manoeuvre and landed again. The spectacle involved technology associated with SpaceX, including cold-gas thrusters and a system designed to help the vehicle move beyond the limitations of ordinary tyre traction. Yes, we have officially reached the point where a car launch looks like something a child would invent after watching too much science fiction.

And the best part? This is not a conventional flying car in the way most of us imagine one. The demonstration showed brief, controlled airborne movement, not a vehicle cruising through the sky like a private aircraft. The final production capabilities still need to be demonstrated and independently verified. That distinction matters, but it does not make the technology any less fascinating.

Think about how absurd the idea sounds when you strip away the branding. Take a vehicle designed to drive on roads. Give it technology inspired by spacecraft. Use compressed gas and thrusters to produce forces beyond ordinary tyre grip. Then try to make the entire thing work in a car that a person can actually buy. There are a thousand ways that could go wrong, and probably a thousand engineers who could explain why the idea is more complicated than it looks.
And yet, somebody is trying to build it. That is the part that caught my attention. Not because I suddenly believe every promise Tesla makes, but because the ambition itself is difficult to ignore.

sections.heading: 2. Love him or hate him, you cannot ignore him.
paragraphs: Elon Musk is one of those people who can turn a completely ordinary day on the internet into an argument about the future of humanity. Mention his name and somebody will tell you he is a genius. Somebody else will tell you he is an idiot. Someone will bring up his politics, someone will bring up his companies, and someone will inevitably post a meme that has been recycled so many times it deserves its own retirement plan.

I understand the criticism. Musk has made ambitious predictions that slipped, and his companies’ announcements deserve scrutiny rather than automatic applause. The Roadster itself is a perfect example. The next-generation version was unveiled in 2017, with earlier delivery expectations passing without the car reaching customers. Now Tesla is talking about production in 2028. That history should absolutely be part of the conversation.

But I also think we sometimes become so invested in disliking a person that we stop being able to examine what they are actually attempting. We turn every new announcement into a referendum on their character. If we like them, we believe the promises. If we dislike them, we dismiss the entire idea before looking at it.

The interesting question is not whether Musk is a good person, a bad person, or the main character of an exceptionally expensive science-fiction film. It is how someone manages to repeatedly place enormous, public bets on ideas that most people would consider absurd.
You do not have to admire everything about a person to recognise that there is something worth studying about the way they operate.

sections.heading: 3. The audacity to imagine something ridiculous
paragraphs: Electric cars existed before Tesla. Rockets existed before SpaceX. Musk did not invent electricity, space travel, or the concept of making ambitious promises on the internet. The more interesting part of his story is how aggressively he has tried to push certain technologies into the public imagination and turn them into businesses.

Tesla helped make electric cars desirable to people who wanted performance and design, not just a vehicle that happened to be electric. SpaceX pursued reusable rockets in an industry where launching a rocket and throwing away much of the hardware had long been an accepted approach. Neither achievement happened because somebody simply woke up one morning, announced a revolutionary idea and watched the universe cooperate.

They required engineers, scientists, technicians, manufacturing teams, investors and an extraordinary amount of work from people whose names most of us will never know. It would be ridiculous to pretend that one man personally builds every machine or that a company’s achievements belong to its CEO alone.

Still, someone has to be willing to make the initial bet. Someone has to convince a team that the difficult thing is worth attempting, find the resources to pursue it and accept that the result might be a very public failure. That ability to turn an ambitious idea into a serious undertaking is what fascinates me.
There is a difference between having a wild idea and building an organisation willing to spend years trying to make it real. The first is easy. The second is where things get interesting.

sections.heading: 4. Balls of steel, or just an unreasonable tolerance for failure?
paragraphs: Imagine telling people that you want to build a rocket company that lands and reuses its boosters. Imagine trying to convince people that electric vehicles can compete on performance and desirability. Now imagine announcing that your sports car is going to use rocket-inspired technology to perform airborne manoeuvres.

Most of us would struggle to explain the idea without adding a nervous laugh at the end. We would soften the language, lower the expectations and make sure nobody could accuse us of taking ourselves too seriously. That way, if the idea failed, we could always say we were only joking.

Musk’s public approach is almost the opposite. He makes enormous claims, attaches his name and companies to them, and allows the entire internet to watch what happens next. That can be a strength when it helps rally people around an ambitious goal. It can also be a weakness when confidence runs ahead of evidence and deadlines become promises that other people are left waiting for.

I do not think the lesson is that everyone should become reckless. Taking risks with other people’s time, money or safety is not automatically courageous. Sometimes it is simply irresponsible. Making a bold claim is not the same as delivering a working product.

But there is something to be said for being willing to look ridiculous while attempting something genuinely difficult. The possibility of embarrassment is enough to stop many people before they have even begun. We would rather have a respectable failure that nobody noticed than an ambitious failure that everybody remembers.

Musk seems unusually willing to accept the second kind. Whether that willingness comes from confidence, stubbornness, an enormous appetite for risk or some combination of all three, it is a big part of why people keep watching.

sections.heading: 5. The future is probably weirder than we think
paragraphs: What excites me about the Roadster is not the idea that we will all be flying to college in Teslas next year. Please. Mumbai traffic is already a multiplayer survival game, and I can only imagine what happens when somebody tries to merge into the sky without using an indicator.

It is the possibility that technologies we currently associate with one industry could eventually find applications somewhere else. Spacecraft use thrusters to manoeuvre without relying on tyres or conventional road traction. A road vehicle incorporating related technology raises fascinating questions about force, control, energy storage, weight, materials and safety. Even if the final application turns out to be a niche performance feature rather than everyday transportation, the engineering challenge is worth examining.

Of course, a demonstration is not proof of practical usefulness. A brief hop is not sustained flight. A prototype is not a production vehicle. A headline-grabbing specification is not an independently verified result. The Roadster still has to prove what it can do outside a carefully staged demonstration, and its planned production timeline has to become reality.

But consider how much of what we now treat as ordinary once belonged to the category of things that sounded absurd. Computers in our pockets. Reusable orbital rockets. Electric vehicles accelerating faster than many supercars. Artificial intelligence generating software, images and conversations that would have looked like science fiction not too long ago.

None of that means every futuristic idea will work. Plenty will not. Some will be technically possible but financially impractical. Others will solve problems nobody actually has. Progress is not a straight line from a wild idea to a wonderful invention; it is a messy collection of experiments, dead ends, improvements and unexpected consequences.

Still, I find it exciting that people are willing to explore the boundaries. Even when an idea does not become the product its creators imagined, the attempt can reveal something useful about what is possible, what is too difficult and what needs to change.

sections.heading: 6. The part that hits closer to home
paragraphs: I think the reason this story stayed with me is that it is not entirely about Elon Musk. It is also about how we treat ambition, especially when it belongs to somebody who has not proved themselves yet.

Think about how many ideas die before anyone even attempts them. A student has a project idea but worries that it is too ambitious. Someone wants to start a company but is terrified of being laughed at. An engineer imagines a different way of solving a problem, then convinces themselves that somebody smarter has probably already tried it. We are very good at rejecting ourselves on behalf of an audience that may not even exist.

And the internet makes this worse. We have turned failure into entertainment. An unfinished project becomes a meme. A delayed launch becomes a punchline. A person who tries something and gets it wrong can end up being remembered for that one moment long after everyone has forgotten the dozens of things they got right.

I am not saying we should stop criticising people or start celebrating every unfinished project. Accountability matters. Competence matters. Finishing what you start matters. At some point, an ambitious idea has to leave the presentation slide and survive contact with reality.
But I do wonder how many of us have become so afraid of looking foolish that we have stopped attempting anything that might make us look foolish in the first place.

As someone who enjoys building projects, I know there is a difference between having an idea that sounds impressive and getting the thing to work. The distance between those two points can be frustrating. There are bugs, compromises, things you misunderstood and things you have to rebuild because your original approach simply was not good enough. Sometimes the result looks nothing like what you imagined when you started.
You can either treat that gap as proof that you should never have tried, or accept that the gap is part of the process. I am still learning to do the latter.

sections.heading: 7. So, does Elon Musk deserve the hype?
paragraphs: Honestly? It depends on which part of the hype we are talking about.

If we are talking about treating every announcement as a guaranteed breakthrough, then no. The Roadster’s long history of delays is a reminder that ambition does not cancel out the need for execution. If we are talking about assuming that one billionaire is personally responsible for every achievement produced by thousands of people, then absolutely not. That version of the story gives too little credit to the people doing the actual work.

But if we are talking about the willingness to pursue technologies that sound ridiculous, attract enormous attention and force people to reconsider what they thought was possible, then I understand the fascination.

I do not need to agree with everything Musk says to find his approach to ambitious engineering interesting. I do not need to believe that every promise will come true to appreciate the people attempting to make difficult things work. And I certainly do not need to turn a complicated human being into either a superhero or a villain to talk about what his companies are trying to achieve.

The Roadster might eventually become a remarkable piece of engineering. It might arrive with fewer capabilities than promised. It might remain a spectacular niche product whose most memorable contribution is a demonstration that looked incredible on a screen. We will have to wait and see.
For now, I am happy to be excited about the possibility while keeping my expectations attached to the evidence.

sections.heading: Anyway, back to the future.
paragraphs: There is something almost funny about the fact that we live in a time when a person can announce a car with rocket-inspired thrusters, demonstrate it briefly leaving the ground and have millions of people around the world arguing about it before the week is over. Somewhere, a science-fiction writer is probably wondering why they bothered making the story more believable.

I do not know whether the future belongs to flying cars, autonomous vehicles, reusable rockets or technologies we have not even figured out how to describe yet. I do know that the future rarely arrives exactly as we imagine it. It shows up in prototypes, failed experiments, awkward first versions and people stubborn enough to keep working on something after the rest of us have decided it looks ridiculous.

So yes, Elon Musk has balls of steel. Or at least an exceptionally high tolerance for public embarrassment and ambitious deadlines. Whether that turns out to be a superpower or a liability depends on what he actually delivers.

But the part I want to take away from all this is simpler. You do not have to worship a person to learn something from what they attempt. You do not have to believe every promise to appreciate the ambition behind a difficult problem. And you do not have to know for certain that an idea will work before you give it a serious chance.
Build the thing. Test the thing. Find out where it breaks. Fix what you can. Admit what does not work. Then decide whether the next attempt is worth making.
And if your next project involves making a car fly, please, for the love of engineering, start with a prototype.

title: To Get Her Is Easy. Together Is Impossible.
subtitle: Five relationships later, I’m still learning what it means to love someone.
excerpt: I have managed to get the girl I wanted. The difficult part, apparently, is figuring out what comes after that. Somewhere between my romantic history, my questionable relationship with my own ego, and my growing respect for single uncles and Salman Khan, I have started wondering whether we have misunderstood what it means to find love.

content.lead: I think I am beginning to understand the appeal of being a single uncle. You know the type. He shows up at his best friend’s house with gifts for the kid, buys them something their parents specifically told them not to buy, plays with them for three hours, and then goes home to enjoy the kind of silence parents would sell a kidney for. No school fees, no sleepless nights, no arguments about screen time. Just vibes. The kid thinks he is the coolest man alive, the parents get a break, and he gets to return to his peaceful little kingdom whenever he wants. Add Salman Khan to the conversation, and suddenly I am wondering whether we have misunderstood the assignment entirely. Maybe marriage is not the final boss of adulthood. Maybe some people really are happier doing their own thing, loving their people, and refusing to participate in the whole circus. And then I remember that this thought is not coming from some enlightened understanding of life. It is coming from someone who has experienced what it feels like to get the girl he wanted and still not make things work. At this point, I am seriously considering that honorary membership in the Association of Cool Single Uncles.

sections.heading: The winning streak that nobody asked for
paragraphs: Here is the funny part. Getting the girl has never really been the problem. I have liked someone, wanted to be with her, and somehow ended up in a relationship with her. The problem has been what happens after the exciting beginning, when the butterflies settle down and two actual human beings have to figure out how to exist together. You would think that wanting someone badly enough would prepare you for the reality of being with them. It does not. Wanting a relationship and knowing how to maintain one are entirely different skills, and I am beginning to suspect that I spent far too long assuming the first would naturally lead to the second.

There is something particularly embarrassing about being good at the beginning of things. The flirting, the excitement, the late-night conversations, the feeling that someone has chosen to let you into a part of their world that nobody else gets to see. Beginnings are generous. They give you possibility without immediately demanding proof that you know what to do with it. You get to imagine the person you could become together before everyday life asks you to actually become that person.

And yes, I know the usual speech about how every failed relationship teaches you something. But recognising a pattern and knowing how to break it are two very different things. You can promise yourself that the next time will be different and still find yourself standing in familiar territory, wondering how you got there again. Eventually, blaming bad timing starts feeling suspiciously convenient. At some point, you have to look at your own role in the story.

sections.heading: My ego and its excellent track record
paragraphs: If I had to nominate one suspect, my ego would be the first person I interrogated. Not because I think I am some cartoon villain who deliberately hurts people, but because ego is much sneakier than that. Sometimes it looks like confidence. Sometimes it looks like having standards. Sometimes it is the little voice that tells you that you should not have to explain yourself, that the other person should simply understand, or that apologising first means losing something.

I wonder how often I have confused being right with making things right. How often the need to explain what I meant has been stronger than the willingness to understand how something I did might have felt to somebody else. It is remarkably easy to love someone in your head, where your intentions are always good and every mistake comes with a perfectly reasonable explanation. It is harder in reality, where your intentions do not erase another person’s experience and being sorry does not magically undo what happened.

I do not want to sit here and pretend I have figured out every mistake I made in every relationship. I have not. The women I have been with are not five interchangeable characters in the story of my personal development. They are people with their own feelings, experiences, and reasons for how things unfolded. Not every ending has to mean that somebody was the villain. I can only speak for my side of the mess, and even that is something I am still trying to understand.

But one question keeps coming back to me: have I sometimes been so busy wanting to be loved that I have not paid enough attention to what it means to make another person feel loved? Those two things sound almost identical until you look at them closely. One is about what you receive. The other asks what you are willing to give, especially when giving it is inconvenient or requires you to admit that you have been acting like an idiot.

You can want someone to stay while making it unnecessarily difficult for them to do so. You can want closeness and still become defensive when someone gets close enough to see you properly. You can want a relationship and treat compromise like a threat to your independence. I am not claiming that every one of these things describes me perfectly. I am asking whether any of them do, because I would rather confront an uncomfortable possibility than keep repeating the same story and call it fate.

sections.heading: Love is not the same as being chosen
paragraphs: There is a particular high that comes with knowing someone you really like likes you back. You are no longer guessing or imagining conversations that might never happen. The person you wanted is there, choosing you too, and for a little while everything feels absurdly simple. It is intoxicating to be wanted by someone you want. There is nothing wrong with enjoying that feeling. We are human beings. Of course we want to be chosen.

But being chosen is only the beginning. Eventually, the novelty settles down. You stop discovering each other exclusively through carefully selected conversations and start encountering the less cinematic parts of being together. You have misunderstandings. You have bad days. You realise that two people can care about each other and still have completely different ideas about what care should look like. You have to talk about things you would rather avoid, and sometimes the conversation you need to have is precisely the one your ego wants you to escape.

I think we spend so much time talking about finding the right person that we forget to ask what happens after we find them. The right person cannot communicate on your behalf, resolve every insecurity you carry, or translate every silence into something reassuring. Eventually, you both have to live with the actual people you are, not just the versions you imagined you would become together.

Sometimes love looks like doing something boring because it matters to the other person. Sometimes it means listening without preparing a defence, admitting you do not know how to handle something, or asking to figure it out together. There is no soundtrack that tells you when to apologise and no grand gesture that automatically fixes what a hundred smaller moments have damaged.

And sometimes, despite both people trying, it still does not work. People can care deeply for each other and remain incompatible. Circumstances change, needs diverge, and two good people can reach a point where staying together hurts more than letting go. I do not want to turn my romantic history into a courtroom where I am both the accused and the judge. The point is not that every ending was entirely my fault. The point is that I am the one person who can take responsibility for the part I played.

sections.heading: Why I understand the single uncle now
paragraphs: There is something comforting about a life that does not have to be measured against a checklist. You do not have to be married by a certain age, have children by another, or prove that your life is complete by fitting it into a shape everyone recognises. You can build friendships that last decades, show up for your family, fall in love if you want to, and decide that marriage is not the destination you need to reach. You can be the person a kid remembers as the coolest uncle in the world without having to become a father yourself.

And honestly, the freedom sounds lovely. There is a certain peace in imagining a life where your decisions belong entirely to you, where you can spend a Sunday doing absolutely nothing without negotiating it with another person, and where your mistakes are yours to deal with. I can understand why the simplicity looks attractive.

But I also have to be careful about the story I tell myself. It is one thing to genuinely prefer being single. It is another to declare relationships overrated because you are tired of confronting the ways you struggle inside them. Independence can be a perfectly good choice, but it can also become a respectable-sounding hiding place for the fear of getting things wrong again. From the outside, those lives might look identical. The difference is what you are running towards and what you might be running away from.

Maybe that is why I find the single uncle such an appealing character. He represents the possibility of a good life outside the conventional script. I do not know his entire story, though. Maybe he is happily single. Maybe he has loved and lost. Maybe he is still figuring it out. Or maybe he just really likes buying his best friend’s kid expensive toys and returning them before bedtime. All of those are perfectly respectable ways to be a person.

sections.heading: The love of your life is not a finish line
paragraphs: The title of this essay sounds pretty definitive. Get the girl, fail at the together part, and apparently spend the rest of your life buying toys for somebody else’s children. But I do not actually know how my story ends. I do not know whom I will meet, what I will learn, or whether the person I eventually build a life with is somebody I have already loved or somebody I have not even met yet. Anyone who claims to know the ending while they are still in the middle of the story is probably trying to sell you something.

What I do know is that the idea of the love of your life can become a dangerous little fantasy if you are not careful. It makes love sound like a person you find, recognise, and then somehow keep forever if the universe approves of your application. But the person you love is still a person. They will change. So will you. The question is not simply whether you found the right person. It is whether you can keep choosing each other as life changes what choosing each other requires.

Even that is not a guarantee. Love is not a reward for personal growth, and marriage is not a certificate proving that you finally became good enough. You can work on yourself and still have relationships that end. You can love somebody honestly and discover that the two of you cannot build the same future. I want to get better at loving someone, not because that will guarantee a happy ending, but because the way I treat another person matters regardless of how the story ends.

Maybe the goal is not to become so good at getting the girl that you eventually secure the perfect ending. Maybe it is to become somebody who can participate in a relationship without turning every disagreement into a contest or every vulnerability into a risk calculation. Somebody who can admit when he is wrong, communicate before resentment does the talking, and understand that being loved does not exempt him from the work of being a good partner.

I want to become that person because whoever I love next deserves more than somebody who enjoys the fact that she chose him. She deserves someone who is interested in the actual work of choosing her back. Not a perfect person who never makes mistakes, but someone willing to recognise them and try to do better. I do not think I need to have myself completely figured out before I deserve love. I just do not want to keep using that as an excuse to avoid figuring myself out.

sections.heading: Anyway, see you at the wedding. Maybe.
paragraphs: There is a chance I end up married. There is a chance I do not. There is a chance I meet somebody who makes me understand things about love that I currently cannot articulate, and a chance that I spend the rest of my life being the uncle who gives children too much chocolate and returns them to their parents before the consequences arrive. I can imagine being happy in either life. I can also imagine being terrified of either life. Apparently, being human means wanting certainty about things that refuse to offer it.

I still believe in love. I think. I believe in finding someone you can be completely ridiculous with, someone who knows the less impressive parts of you and chooses to stay, someone with whom ordinary life becomes a little less ordinary. But believing in love and knowing how to practise it are not the same thing. One is a feeling. The other is something you keep learning, particularly when your ego would rather you pretend you already know everything.

I have spent enough time wondering why things did not work out to realise that I do not want my next relationship to become another exercise in proving something to myself. I do not want to treat love like an achievement to unlock or marriage like evidence that I finally got my life together. I want to be able to show up, communicate, admit when I am wrong, and make room for another person without treating every uncomfortable moment as a threat to who I am. Whether that eventually leads to marriage is a different question.

I am twenty, and I have no business pretending to have life figured out. Maybe I will look back at this essay years from now and cringe at how confidently I wrote about something I was still learning to understand. I hope I do. I hope the person reading this in the future has learned something I have not learned yet.

Until then, I will keep the single uncles in high regard, continue respecting Salman Khan’s commitment to doing things his own way, and try not to mistake the ability to win somebody over for the ability to build a life with them. If love happens again, I hope I meet it with a little less pride and a little more courage. And if I end up being the cool uncle instead, I promise the kid is getting the expensive toy. Their parents can deal with the rest.

title: The Fear of Missing-Out
subtitle: At some point, I just stopped giving a fuck.
excerpt: Someone is at a party. Someone got an internship. Someone is travelling, falling in love, making money, living their best life. Meanwhile, there is a new movie to watch, a new technology to learn, and another LinkedIn announcement reminding you that you are apparently falling behind. At some point, I got tired of feeling like I was missing my own life.

content.lead: I think I got tired of wanting to be everywhere, know everything, do everything, and somehow become everyone at once. Tired of seeing people live lives I was not living and feeling like I had somehow fucked up mine. Tired of turning an ordinary Tuesday into an existential crisis because someone my age had achieved something I had not. And somewhere along the way, I started giving less of a fuck, because honestly, how much of this shit are we supposed to keep up with?

sections.heading: Everyone Is Doing Something. Apparently.
paragraphs: Open Instagram. Someone is travelling. Someone is in a relationship. Someone is having the time of their life at a concert, screaming their lungs out, while someone else is posting a photo dump captioned "life lately" with pictures that look like they were directed by Christopher Nolan.
Fine. Good for them. Now open LinkedIn.

Someone got an internship. Someone won a hackathon. Someone got a placement package that makes you question every academic and career decision you have ever made. Someone built a startup, launched an AI product, and announced their latest achievement with a post that begins with "I am humbled and honoured to share..."

And then there is you, sitting in your room, wondering what the fuck you are doing with your life. You were perfectly happy five minutes ago, but apparently, a stranger getting an internship has turned your entire existence into a performance review.

The funny thing is that you do not even necessarily want what they have. You might not want to go to that party, work at that company, build that startup, or travel to that destination. But the moment you realise someone else is doing something you are not, you start wondering whether you should be doing it too.

We have somehow managed to turn other people’s happiness into evidence against our own. Their success becomes a reminder of everything we have not accomplished, and their experiences become a list of things we are apparently missing out on.

And you know what makes it worse? You can understand how ridiculous this is and still feel it anyway. You can tell yourself that everyone has their own timeline, that social media only shows the highlights, and that comparison is pointless, but one particularly well-written LinkedIn post can still ruin a perfectly good afternoon.

sections.heading: Bhai, There Is a New Movie Every Week.
paragraphs: This is not even limited to social media anymore. There is simply too much happening in the world, and somehow, we have convinced ourselves that we are supposed to keep up with all of it.

A new movie comes out, and suddenly everyone is talking about it. You see reviews, edits, discussions, theories, spoilers, and people calling it the greatest cinematic experience of their lives. And there you are, thinking, "Oh shit, I have not watched it yet. Am I missing something?"

Then another movie comes out before you have even found the time to watch the first one. Someone recommends a series. Someone else tells you that you absolutely must watch this documentary. A film you have wanted to see for months finally becomes available, but now you feel guilty watching it because there are five other things you could be doing instead.

At this point, will my life actually end if I do not watch the new movie? Will I lose my ability to appreciate cinema? Will Christopher Nolan personally come to my house and revoke my movie-watching privileges? Haha.

And it is not just movies. There is always a new album, a new book, a new game, a new trend, a new place everyone is visiting, or some cultural moment that apparently everybody experienced except you. You can spend your entire life consuming things and still barely scratch the surface of what exists.

The same thing happens with technology. A new framework arrives, a new AI tool becomes popular, and suddenly you feel like everything you learned last month is obsolete. You start exploring one thing, discover three more things you should learn, and before you have properly understood any of them, the internet has already moved on to something else.

I genuinely want to know when we are supposed to use all this knowledge, watch all these movies, enjoy all this music, and actually live our lives. Are we supposed to keep consuming things until we die? Is there some final level where I unlock the ability to watch every film ever made while simultaneously mastering every programming language?
Because if there is, I would like to know where to register.

sections.heading: The LinkedIn Olympics
paragraphs: I genuinely think LinkedIn deserves its own category of psychological warfare. You open the app to look for opportunities and, fifteen minutes later, you are questioning whether you have wasted your entire life.

Someone completed an internship. Someone got selected for a prestigious programme. Someone published research. Someone attended a conference. Someone is building their fourth startup while still in college, and you are wondering whether your weekend project is even worth finishing.

And suddenly, every single thing you have not done becomes urgent. You should be applying to more internships, building more projects, learning another language, participating in another hackathon, networking with more people, and somehow maintaining a social life while doing all of this.

You start treating your life like a checklist that someone else is constantly updating. Every achievement you see adds another item to the list, and every day you do not complete it feels like another day wasted.

But the list never ends. There will always be someone doing more, learning faster, earning earlier, or achieving something you have not even thought about yet. You could spend your entire life trying to catch up and still find yourself behind someone.

And the worst part is that ambition, which should be something exciting, starts feeling like anxiety. You stop building things because you enjoy building them and start building things because you are afraid of being left behind. You stop learning out of curiosity and start learning because you are terrified that the world will move on without you.

I do not want to become someone who measures every hour by how productive it was or every experience by how useful it will look on a résumé. I want to do meaningful work, achieve things I am proud of, and build a career I care about. But I also want to remember that I am a human being, not a LinkedIn profile that needs a new achievement every week.
Good for everyone who is doing incredible things. Genuinely. But their progress should not have to become the reason I stop appreciating mine.

sections.heading: Then One Day, I Just Got Tired.
paragraphs: I do not remember the exact moment it happened. There was no dramatic realisation, no cinematic background score, and no sunset where I suddenly understood the meaning of life. I think I just got tired of feeling like I was constantly late to something.

Tired of feeling guilty for staying in when other people were going out. Tired of feeling behind because somebody else was ahead. Tired of treating every opportunity I did not take as some irreversible mistake that would haunt me until the end of time.
I started asking myself a question I probably should have asked much earlier: do I actually want to do this, or am I just afraid of being the only person who did not?

Because there is a difference between wanting to experience something and being terrified of missing it. One comes from curiosity, and the other comes from panic. One makes you excited about life, while the other makes you feel like life is happening somewhere else and you are desperately trying to get there.

I still want to travel, build things, meet people, watch great movies, discover new music, and have stories worth telling. I want to try new things and take opportunities that excite me. I am not trying to become some enlightened monk who has transcended all human desires.

I just do not want to chase experiences because somebody else had them first. I do not want to watch a movie just because everyone is talking about it, attend an event just because I am afraid of missing out, or learn a technology without even knowing why I want to learn it.

Sometimes I want to stay home. Sometimes I want to spend an entire evening watching something stupid. Sometimes I want to do absolutely nothing productive without feeling like I owe the world an explanation for it.
And honestly, that should be allowed. I should be able to enjoy my own life without constantly checking whether somebody else is enjoying theirs more.

sections.heading: You Cannot Live Every Life.
paragraphs: Here is the uncomfortable bit: you are going to miss out, no matter what you do. You will miss parties, movies, friendships that might have happened, opportunities you did not recognise until they were gone, and places you might never get the chance to visit.

You will discover artists years after everyone else has stopped listening to them. You will watch a famous film for the first time and wonder why nobody told you about it earlier, only to realise that people probably did and you simply did not have the time. You will hear about an opportunity after applications have closed and see someone else get something you once wanted.

And sometimes, you will regret it. That is part of being alive. There will always be another version of your life that you could have lived, another choice you could have made, and another experience you could have had if only you had been somewhere else at the right time.

But you cannot experience everything. You cannot watch every movie, attend every event, learn every skill, know every person, and take every opportunity. You could live a hundred years and still leave this world with a thousand things left undone.

We talk about FOMO as if missing out is the problem, but sometimes the real problem is believing that we should be able to have everything. We have confused having options with being obligated to explore every single one of them.

Every choice means choosing something over something else. Spend an evening with your family, and you might miss a party. Work on a project, and you might miss a movie. Take a break, and someone else might get ahead. You cannot always know whether you made the perfect decision, but you can stop treating every alternative as a life you have lost.

Maybe growing up is realising that a meaningful life is not measured by how many things you manage to squeeze into it. Maybe it is also about the things you deliberately leave out, the opportunities you let pass, and the experiences you decide are simply not for you.

sections.heading: I Still Give a Fuck. Just About Different Things.
paragraphs: Let me be honest. I have not magically stopped comparing myself to people. I still get jealous sometimes, still wonder whether I am doing enough, and still see someone achieving something incredible and have that brief, uncomfortable thought about what I might be doing wrong.

I am human, unfortunately. But I am trying to stop treating every feeling of being left behind as an emergency. Someone got an opportunity I did not get? Good for them. Someone is having the time of their life somewhere I have never been? I hope they have a great time. Someone is ahead of me in a race I did not even consciously sign up for? Good for fucking them.

Not because I am better than them, and not because I have given up on my own ambitions, but because I am beginning to understand that another person’s life is not a referendum on mine. Their timeline is not a deadline for me, and their achievements do not automatically turn my own efforts into failures.

I want to care about the people I love, the work I do, and the things I create. I want to learn because I am curious, watch movies because I love cinema, and pursue opportunities because they genuinely excite me. I want to be present when I am with someone instead of mentally checking whether I could be somewhere better.

I also want to be okay with not knowing everything. There will be technologies I never learn, books I never read, movies I never watch, and conversations about things I know absolutely nothing about. I can live with that. I do not need to have an opinion on everything or participate in every conversation to justify my existence.

And if I miss something important, I can acknowledge it and move on. If I make a mistake, I can learn from it. If someone else succeeds, I can congratulate them without turning their success into a personal failure. Life is already complicated enough without making every ordinary experience a competition.
I still care about my future. I still want to achieve things and make something of myself. I just do not want the fear of falling behind to become the only reason I keep moving forward.

sections.heading: Anyway, What Was I Saying?
paragraphs: I think there is something quietly beautiful about being okay with missing out. Not in a performative, "I am protecting my peace" way, and not in a way where you pretend you do not care about anyone or anything. I mean being comfortable enough with your own choices that you do not need to justify every single thing you do or do not do.

There will always be another party, another trip, another achievement, another movie, another trend, another technology, and another notification telling you that somebody, somewhere, is doing something you are not. The world is not going to run out of things to make you feel behind, so perhaps you have to stop giving every one of them that much power over you.

I am not saying that I have figured this out. Tomorrow, I might open Instagram and immediately feel like shit again. I might open LinkedIn and wonder whether I should have worked harder. I might discover that everyone has watched a movie I have never heard of, and for five seconds, I might genuinely feel like I have failed as a human being.

But maybe I will catch myself. Maybe I will put the phone down, return to whatever I was doing, and remember that the life I am living is not supposed to be a complete collection of everything the world has to offer.

There is so much I am going to miss in this lifetime. So many places I will never see, people I will never meet, things I will never learn, and experiences I will never have. For once, I do not want that thought to scare me. I want it to remind me that I have limited time, and I would rather spend it enjoying a few things properly than anxiously chasing a million things I might never get to experience.

So, if a new movie comes out and I do not watch it immediately, I will probably survive. If someone announces an achievement on LinkedIn, I can be happy for them and continue with my day. If a new technology arrives, I can decide whether it is worth my time instead of panicking because the internet has decided it is the future.
I do not need to be everywhere. I do not need to know everything. I do not need to turn every passing interest into a lifelong pursuit or every missed opportunity into a tragedy.
I just want to live the life that is actually here, with the people who are actually here, doing things that actually matter to me.

And if something exciting happens while I am busy doing that, someone can tell me about it later. I will catch up when I can, and if I never catch up, I guess I will just have to live with the terrible consequences of not watching one more movie.
Honestly, I think I will be fine.

title: Am I an Atheist?
subtitle: On God, the business my family built around Him, and the questions I was never afraid to ask
excerpt: My family has spent generations selling things people buy to worship God. And here I am, questioning what it means to believe in Him. Sometimes, the irony is impossible to ignore.

content.lead: Am I an atheist? I think about this quite a lot. Whenever I visit a temple and see people praying, making offerings, or performing rituals, a question quietly appears in my head: for whom? It is not that I do not believe in God. I do. I just wonder whether my God looks a little different from yours.

sections.heading: The Irony Is Not Lost on Me
paragraphs: My family has a business that sells pooja-related items. If I join it someday, I will be the fourth generation to carry it forward.

Think about that for a moment. Four generations of a family building something around people’s faith in God, and somewhere in that same family is a person asking whether he even understands God correctly.
The irony is almost funny.

I have grown up around things people buy to please God, to seek His blessings, or to feel closer to Him. And I have often wondered about the money we spend trying to please someone we believe is above us, especially when that same money could sometimes help someone who is struggling right here on Earth.

I am not saying that the business is wrong or that people should stop practising their faith. This is my family’s livelihood, and I respect what generations before me have built. But being close to something does not mean you should never question it.
Perhaps that is exactly why I question it.

sections.heading: My Grandmother Prays. My Parents Let Me Think.
paragraphs: My grandmother fears God. For her, faith is something to be respected, something that deserves devotion. I have seen a different relationship with religion through my parents. They never forced me to pray or made belief feel like an obligation.
They left room for me to figure things out myself.

And I think that matters more than we realise. When belief is forced upon you, you might learn the rituals before you ever understand their meaning. But when you are allowed to ask questions, you get the chance to discover what faith means to you, if anything at all.

Maybe that is where education comes in. Not necessarily to make someone religious or irreligious, but to teach them to think, question, examine, and arrive at their own understanding instead of accepting something simply because it has always been done that way.
I can respect my grandmother’s faith without having to experience God exactly as she does. And I can love my family’s traditions without surrendering my right to question them.

sections.heading: Three Books, One Word
paragraphs: I have read the Bhagavad Gita, the Quran, and the Bible. They are different books, born from different traditions, and I would never claim they teach exactly the same things.
But one thing kept standing out to me: humanity.
Compassion. Humility. Helping others. Being responsible for the way we treat people.
So why do we sometimes spend so much time trying to please God that we forget the people around us?

If I see milk or food that could instead help someone in need, I will always find myself asking whether helping that person might be a more meaningful offering. The hungry person does not need to know which religion I follow. They need food.

I believe someone above me might want me to succeed. But I cannot spend my entire life praying for success and refuse to work for it. I cannot ask for a kinder world while contributing nothing to making it kinder.
If there is a God watching me, I hope He wants me to try.

sections.heading: So, Am I an Atheist?
paragraphs: I honestly do not know.

I believe in something greater than myself, but I question the ways we try to understand it. I respect people who pray, but I do not want prayer to become a substitute for effort. I value tradition, but I do not think tradition should be beyond questioning.
Maybe I am a believer. Maybe I am not. Maybe I am still figuring it out, and that is perfectly fine.

I do not think I am superior to anyone for asking these questions. I have my own flaws, my own failures, and plenty of things I need to work on. I am not writing this because I have figured life out. I am writing because I have not.
And perhaps the strangest part is that I can be part of a fourth-generation pooja-items business, grow up around religion, respect my grandmother’s devotion, and still wonder what God means to me.
Maybe that is what education has given me: not all the answers, but the courage to ask questions I might otherwise have been afraid to ask.
I do not know if God is watching.
But I know people are hurting. I know there are people who need food, kindness, opportunity, and someone willing to care.
And I would rather spend my life trying to give them some of that than spend it worrying about whether I have the right label for my beliefs.
So, am I an atheist?
Maybe the answer can wait. I have people to be kind to.
